title: Generosity
hook: an open heart and an open hand

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was zerizut, and your line was promptly. What good thing did you do now instead of later? Today, the heart and the hand. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-five.

The craftsmen building the Tabernacle put down their tools and go to Moses with a problem. It isn't a shortage. It's the opposite. Morning after morning, the people keep bringing gifts: gold and silver, blue and purple yarn, wood, skins, spun goats' hair. There is more than the work needs. So Moses sends word through the whole camp: no one bring any more. And Exodus adds: "So the people were restrained from bringing." An appeal, called off because it worked. Today's word is what was moving all those hands.
screen: `THE CRAFTSMEN GO TO MOSES.` → `MORE THAN ENOUGH.` → `STOP BRINGING.`

segments.voice: Nedivut. Generosity: an open heart and an open hand. Turn it four ways. First, the heart comes first. When the collection began, the call in Exodus went out to "whosoever is of a willing heart." Not to the richest. Not to the ones who owed the most. The gifts are called nedavah, a freewill offering: given because a heart moved, not because a bill came due. Generosity, in this picture, is giving that rises from inside. Second, the hand follows. Deuteronomy, speaking of a neighbor in need, tells Israel not to harden the heart or shut the hand, but to open the hand to the poor. Heart and hand come in the same breath there. A soft heart with a closed hand is only a feeling. An open hand with a hard heart is only a transaction. Third, the trait under the duty. Jewish law treats tzedakah, giving to those in need, as an obligation, owed whether you feel like it or not. Some Mussar teachers describe nedivut as the trait underneath: the inner readiness that makes giving glad instead of grudging. The law says what to give. The trait shapes how it leaves your hand. Fourth, it isn't only money. Exodus tells of women who spun yarn with their own hands and brought what they had spun. Gold sat next to goats' hair in that collection. Time, attention, a meal, a skill, a word of praise you could have kept to yourself: all of it can be brought. And it follows yesterday's zeal: the people didn't wait to be asked twice.
screen: `WHOSOEVER IS OF A WILLING HEART.` · `DON'T SHUT THE HAND.` · `THE TRAIT UNDER THE DUTY.` · `GOLD NEXT TO GOATS' HAIR.` · then, large: `OPEN HEART, OPEN HAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give something today. Settle, and breathe. Notice your hands resting in your lap or on the table. Turn them palm up, and leave them open. Now ask what you have that someone else could use. Not only money. An hour. A ride. A book you've finished. A skill. Praise you've been holding back. Let one gift and one person come to mind together. Then check the heart: is this given gladly? If it isn't yet, make it smaller until it is. If you pray, you can hold the person in your prayer as you decide. The bell holds the time.
Nedivut. Generosity: the willing heart behind the freewill gift, and the open hand that follows it. Today's word.
Your line: open hand. Today, give the gift you chose in the quiet, and give it before the day closes. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Some Jewish homes keep a tzedakah box and drop coins in before Shabbat, and Mussar students work on nedivut by noticing whether their giving comes gladly or grudgingly.
